sweep_summary: Only one title-keyword item exists for tila1239: Turnbull 2017 (JIPA 47(3):251-282, doi:10.1017/S0025100316000384), already listed and already. It is about the Acazulco variety, not Tilapa proper: one lexically placed prominent ('tonic') syllable per word, prefixes pre-tonic, tonic syllables longer/louder/higher; Turnbull calls it a possible 'pitch accent' system and explicitly does not extend it to Tilapa. It refines rather than contradicts the catalog's set by morphology coding (stem prominence with affixal/proclitic material outside), while showing that within-stem position is lexical in Acazulco citation nouns. The best direct stress statement read in this search of works with stress in the title is Hernández-Green 2015 (CIESAS dissertation, open, held by the project since 9/16): first syllable of native words is the prominent, longest syllable, foot ˈσσ, TAM proclitics unaccented — confirming the classification and recommended as co-primary for the languoid, but it does not supersede Palancar 2012, which remains the only statement on Tilapa proper. Nothing new is left to acquire for this item.

new_statements.quote: La mayoría de las palabras nativas tienen una estructura monosilábica o bisilábica como en (10a) y (10b). En estas palabras, el tono léxico está asociado con la primera (o única) sílaba, que es la sílaba prominente. ... En el caso del otomí de Acazulco, el peso de la sílaba está relacionado directamente con su duración: la sílaba más larga corresponde a la sílaba prominente. La sílaba prominente en monosílabos es, evidentemente, la única sílaba, mientras que en bisílabos es la primera sílaba. ... podemos decir que el pie métrico básico de la lengua es ˈσσ.
new_statements.translation: Most native words are monosyllabic or disyllabic as in (10a) and (10b). In these words the lexical tone is associated with the first (or only) syllable, which is the prominent syllable. ... In Acazulco Otomi, syllable weight is directly related to duration: the longest syllable is the prominent syllable. The prominent syllable in monosyllables is obviously the only syllable, while in disyllables it is the first syllable. ... we can say that the basic metrical foot of the language is ˈσσ. (fn. 13: in a Praat sample of 133 disyllables the second syllable averages 61.4% of the first syllable's duration.)
new_statements.citation: Hernández-Green, Néstor. 2015. Morfosintaxis verbal del otomí de Acazulco. Tesis de doctorado, CIESAS, México (x+592 pp.). Open repository:https://ciesas.repositorioinstitucional.mx/jspui/handle/1015/134

new_statements.reading: First-hand, instrumentally supported statement that word prominence in the Acazulco variety is fixed on the first syllable of the (native) word/stem, that lexical tone anchors there, that each member of an adjective+noun sequence keeps its own first-syllable accent while true compounds take one primary accent on the first element, and that the preverbal TAM markers lack primary accent and are proclitics. That is stem-initial prominence with the proclitic cluster outside, the same configuration the catalog codes set by morphology from Palancar 2012's parenthetical on inflected verbs; it extends the rule to nouns. It sits in tension with Turnbull 2017 (same variety), whose citation-form nouns show a lexically placed tonic syllable (second syllable in roughly 38% of disyllables); Turnbull's finding concerns tone anchoring in isolation forms rather than a stress rule, and he does not claim a competing stress placement.

tone_statements.citation: Palancar, Enrique L. 2024. The Oto-Pamean languages. In Søren Wichmann (ed.), The Languages and Linguistics of Mexico and Northern Central America: A Comprehensive Guide (The World of Linguistics), 511-554. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton. doi:10.1515/9783110421705-011. (HAL hal-01493977, author file '', record dated 2025.)
tone_statements.quote: Like other Oto-Manguean languages, Oto-Pamean languages are tonal, but their tonal systems are basic. Pamean languages have a minimal low/high opposition which reflects the old system. … Otomian developed an ascending tone in lexical roots (i.e. it is neither present in affixes nor stem formatives). Again minimal pairs based on tone are rare. The triplet in (8) is exceptional. … (8) /H/ khí+ni ‘facial hair’ E.OTO /HL/ khǐ+ni ‘flat stone for grinding’ /L/ khi+ni ‘corn-dough’ In Oto-Pamean, tone basically works at a lexical level, but it plays an occasional role in inflection.
tone_statements.locator: author-version pp. 5-6, sec. 1 'An overview of the phonology', tone paragraphs with exx. (6)-(8); Acazulco tone inversion at sec. 5.3, author pp. 23-24
tone_statements.summary: Survey: Otomi languages have high, low and an ascending tone, the ascending one only in lexical roots; tonal minimal pairs rare; floating high marks 3rd possessor; Acazulco shows root H~L inversion.

tone_statements.citation: Hernández-Green, Néstor. 2019. Inflectional verb classes in Acazulco Otomi. Amerindia 41: 273-322. doi:10.56551/htwg4319.
tone_statements.quote: The tone stem alternants are concerned with the suprasegmental, i.e. tonal mutations of the verb stem. In such mutations, the tone of the stem changes to either low or high tone. … In those tables, only changes from high/rising to low tone were shown, for the sake of simplicity. … Tone changes occur under these conditions: all verbs in (34) are pronounced with a high tone, whatever their “lexical” tone is; a low tone is observed in all the verb forms in (35), whether their lexical tone is low, high, or rising.
tone_statements.locator: Sec. 3.3 'Tone stem alternants', pp. 302, 305 and 307 (with Tables 22-24 and exx. 32-35)
tone_statements.summary: Verb stems carry a lexical low, high or rising (LH) tone; in Class I-II paradigm cells the stem tone mutates to low (default) or high depending on suffixes/enclitics; no TBU or stress rule given.

tone_statements.citation: Hernández-Green, Néstor. 2017. Relatos de tradición oral en otomí de San Jerónimo Acazulco. Revista de Literaturas Populares XVII(2): 281-305.
tone_statements.quote: El tono bajo (representado con vocal sin diacrítico, como a) corresponde al registro más grave de tonía, mientras que el tono alto (representado con un acento agudo sobre la vocal, como á) es el registro más agudo. El tono ascendente (representado por el acento circunflejo inverso sobre la vocal, como ǎ) tiene un contorno de tonía que puede ir de bajo a alto, o bien de medio a alto.
tone_statements.translation: The low tone (written as a vowel without diacritic, a) corresponds to the lowest pitch register, while the high tone (written with an acute accent on the vowel, á) is the highest register. The rising tone (written with the inverted circumflex on the vowel, ǎ) has a pitch contour that can go from low to high, or from mid to high.
tone_statements.locator: Section 'La lengua yühü', last paragraph before Tabla 1 'Ortografía práctica hñähñu'
tone_statements.summary: Acazulco Otomi (yühü): three tones - low, high, rising (rising realised L-to-H or M-to-H); marked orthographically (unmarked / acute / caron).

tone_statements.citation: Hernández-Green, Néstor. 2016 [issued Dec 2017]. Yu̠ tú̠xpu̠ru̠: Misteriosas figurillas de barro de San Jerónimo Acazulco. Tlalocan XXI: 19-48. doi:10.19130/iifl.tlalocan.2016.442.
tone_statements.quote: Se trata de una lengua tonal (tonos b, a, ba) de marcación en el núcleo, con un importante número de rasgos de verbo inicial. [...] (p.22) La representación del tono se ejemplifica con la grafía <a>. [...] Una tilde sobre el signo de igual (=́) en la línea de análisis morfémico indica la propagación del tono alto a través de frontera entre clíticos.
tone_statements.translation: It is a tonal language (tones L, H, LH) with head marking and a considerable number of verb-initial traits. [...] The representation of tone is exemplified with the letter <a>. [...] An accent over the equals sign in the morphemic-analysis line indicates the spreading of high tone across a boundary between clitics.
tone_statements.locator: Sections 'La lengua yühü' and 'Notas sobre la ortografía práctica y el interlineado'
tone_statements.summary: Acazulco Otomi: three tones (low, high, rising); high-tone spreading across clitic boundaries noted; low-tone verb-stem alternant glossed in texts.

tone_statements.citation: Palancar, Enrique L. 2016. A typology of tone and inflection: A view from the Oto-Manguean languages of Mexico. In Enrique L. Palancar & Jean Léo Léonard (eds.), Tone and Inflection: New Facts and New Perspectives (Trends in Linguistics), 109-140. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton. doi:10.1515/9783110452754-006. (HAL hal-01493968, author file open.)
tone_statements.quote: For example, Otomi languages (Oto-Pamean) have three tones, but only two are relevant for our purposes: high (represented with an acute accent) and low (not represented). … The third tone is a raising tone that is not found in inflectional formatives, but only found in lexical roots. … Acazulco Otomi (Oto-Pamean) also has two tones involved in inflection: high (represented with an acute accent) and low (not represented). … Shading indicates slabs in the paradigm where the lexical tone of the stem is altered, in this case changed to a low tone.
tone_statements.locator: Sec. 2 (author-version p. 3) with fn. 4 (p. 4), and Sec. 4.2 (p. 9, before Table 5); pp. 109-140 of the volume, page numbers not shown in this author version
tone_statements.summary: Otomi languages have three tones: high, low, and a rising tone found only in roots; a floating possessor high lands on the preceding mora; in Acazulco, stem tone (H vs L) marks verb inflection class.

tone_statements.citation: Palancar, Enrique L. 2016. Description grammaticale, comparaison typologique et approche théorique. De l'otomi à d'autres langues otomangues. Mémoire d'habilitation à diriger des recherches (HDR), INALCO, Paris (soutenue 2016-12-06; vol. I open on HAL tel-01424497).
tone_statements.quote: Il y a trois tons à otomi: bas (non représenté), haut (représenté par l’accent aigu) et ascendant. Le ton joue un rôle mineur dans la fabrication de contrastes grammaticaux. Dans ce travail, le ton est seulement représenté dans les formatifs flexionnels, car ce sont les seuls éléments grammaticaux qui peuvent contraster en ton entre ton haut et ton bas (voir les exemples 10 et 11, dans les pages 102-103).
tone_statements.translation: There are three tones in Otomi: low (not represented), high (represented by the acute accent) and rising. Tone plays a minor role in making grammatical contrasts. In this work tone is only represented on the inflectional formatives, since these are the only grammatical elements that can contrast in tone between high tone and low tone (see examples 10 and 11, pp. 102-103).
tone_statements.locator: p. 14, footnote 7 (ch. 2, sec. 2.1 'Introduction à la grammaire otomie'); see also p. 100 (floating H, Otomi languages), pp. 102-103 exx. 10-11 (otomi du nord/SIT) and p. 107 Tableau 29 (Acazulco)
tone_statements.summary: Three tones (low, high, rising), stated for Otomi generally and marked on Tilapa formatives; formatives contrast only high vs low; a floating high tone marks 3rd-person possessor in Otomi languages.

tone_statements.citation: Green, Néstor H. [Hernández-Green, Néstor]. 2011. Surgimiento de formas no finitas (FNF) en otomí de Acazulco. In Memorias del V Congreso de Idiomas Indígenas de Latinoamérica (CILLA V), 6-8 de octubre de 2011, University of Texas at Austin. Austin: AILLA. 28 pp.
tone_statements.quote: El otomí hablado en San Jerónimo Acazulco es una lengua tonal (alto A, bajo B y ascendente BA), en la que el tono tiene funciones tanto léxicas (tö́htá ‘tío’ vs. tö̀htá ‘esposo, viejo’) como flexivas (ngi nǜ ‘verías’ vs. ngi nǘ ‘vería (él)’. Es una lengua de marcación en el núcleo, cuyos verbos reciben marcas de referencia cruzada con Sujeto y Objeto.
tone_statements.translation: The Otomi spoken in San Jerónimo Acazulco is a tonal language (high A, low B and rising BA), in which tone has both lexical functions (tö́htá 'uncle' vs. tö̀htá 'husband, old man') and inflectional ones (ngi nǜ 'you would see' vs. ngi nǘ 'he would see'). It is a head-marking language whose verbs take cross-reference markers for Subject and Object.
tone_statements.summary: Three tones, high, low and rising (BA), with lexical and inflectional minimal pairs; suffixed incorporated nouns lose inherent tone and accent, juxtaposed ones keep both. No fuller tone analysis.

tone_statements.quote: 1. There are two tones: /H/ and /HL/. 2. Each lexical word has one and only one tone, which is lexically associated with one and only one syllable (the 'tonic' syllable). [...] 3. Post-tonic syllables have the same tone as the tonic syllable (rightward spreading). 4. Syllables immediately preceding the tonic syllable are realized with a low tone; all other pre-tonic syllables are realized with a high tone. (pp. 261-262) [...] Compared to non-tonic syllables, syllables with /HL/ tone are longer and have greater intensity and f0 on the vowel; and syllables with /H/ have more consistently tense vowels, produced with greater vocal effort. The generalization here is that the tonic syllables have greater acoustic prominence, manifested through a variety of acoustic means, than do the non-tonic syllables. In this respect, the tonal system of SJAO can be said to be more similar to that of Swedish than Japanese. (pp. 272-273) [...] SJAO is argued to feature one prosodically prominent syllable per word (as per Leon & Swadesh 1949); nevertheless, these tonic syllables contrast in underlying tone (as per Sinclair & Pike 1948). sources.quote: The tone stem alternants are concerned with the suprasegmental, i.e. tonal mutations of the verb stem. In such mutations, the tone of the stem changes to either low or high tone. … In those tables, only changes from high/rising to low tone were shown, for the sake of simplicity. … Tone changes occur under these conditions: all verbs in (34) are pronounced with a high tone, whatever their “lexical” tone is; a low tone is observed in all the verb forms in (35), whether their lexical tone is low, high, or rising.
sources.locator: Sec. 3.3 'Tone stem alternants', pp. 302, 305 and 307 (with Tables 22-24 and exx. 32-35)
sources.note: Verb stems carry a lexical low, high or rising (LH) tone; in Class I-II paradigm cells the stem tone mutates to low (default) or high depending on suffixes/enclitics; no TBU or stress rule given.

sources.citation: Hernández-Green, Néstor. 2017. Relatos de tradición oral en otomí de San Jerónimo Acazulco. Revista de Literaturas Populares XVII(2): 281-305.
sources.quote: El tono bajo (representado con vocal sin diacrítico, como a) corresponde al registro más grave de tonía, mientras que el tono alto (representado con un acento agudo sobre la vocal, como á) es el registro más agudo. El tono ascendente (representado por el acento circunflejo inverso sobre la vocal, como ǎ) tiene un contorno de tonía que puede ir de bajo a alto, o bien de medio a alto.
sources.locator: Section 'La lengua yühü', last paragraph before Tabla 1 'Ortografía práctica hñähñu'
sources.note: Introduction 'La lengua yühü' (pp.281-282) places the language in the tonal Oto-Manguean stock and, before the orthography table (Tabla 1, p.283), states the tone inventory used to transcribe the texts: three tones - low (unmarked vowel, lowest pitch register), high (acute accent, highest register) and rising (inverted circumflex/caron), the rising tone having a contour from low to high or from mid to high. The two tone-marked narrative texts follow (pp.284-305). First-hand (author's fieldwork), brief, no analysis of tone placement or sandhi.

sources.citation: Palancar, Enrique L. 2016. A typology of tone and inflection: A view from the Oto-Manguean languages of Mexico. In Enrique L. Palancar & Jean Léo Léonard (eds.), Tone and Inflection: New Facts and New Perspectives (Trends in Linguistics), 109-140. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton. doi:10.1515/9783110452754-006. (HAL hal-01493968, author file open.)
sources.quote: For example, Otomi languages (Oto-Pamean) have three tones, but only two are relevant for our purposes: high (represented with an acute accent) and low (not represented). … The third tone is a raising tone that is not found in inflectional formatives, but only found in lexical roots. … Acazulco Otomi (Oto-Pamean) also has two tones involved in inflection: high (represented with an acute accent) and low (not represented). … Shading indicates slabs in the paradigm where the lexical tone of the stem is altered, in this case changed to a low tone.
sources.locator: Sec. 2 (author-version p. 3) with fn. 4 (p. 4), and Sec. 4.2 (p. 9, before Table 5); pp. 109-140 of the volume, page numbers not shown in this author version
sources.note: Otomi languages have three tones: high, low, and a rising tone found only in roots; a floating possessor high lands on the preceding mora; in Acazulco, stem tone (H vs L) marks verb inflection class.

sources.quote: Il y a trois tons à otomi: bas (non représenté), haut (représenté par l’accent aigu) et ascendant. Le ton joue un rôle mineur dans la fabrication de contrastes grammaticaux. Dans ce travail, le ton est seulement représenté dans les formatifs flexionnels, car ce sont les seuls éléments grammaticaux qui peuvent contraster en ton entre ton haut et ton bas (voir les exemples 10 et 11, dans les pages 102-103).

tone.translation: There are three tones in Otomi: low (not represented), high (represented by the acute accent) and rising. Tone plays a minor role in making grammatical contrasts. In this work tone is only represented on the inflectional formatives, since these are the only grammatical elements that can contrast in tone between high tone and low tone (see examples 10 and 11, pp. 102-103).

sources.quote: El otomí hablado en San Jerónimo Acazulco es una lengua tonal (alto A, bajo B y ascendente BA), en la que el tono tiene funciones tanto léxicas (tö́htá ‘tío’ vs. tö̀htá ‘esposo, viejo’) como flexivas (ngi nǜ ‘verías’ vs. ngi nǘ ‘vería (él)’. Es una lengua de marcación en el núcleo, cuyos verbos reciben marcas de referencia cruzada con Sujeto y Objeto.
sources.note: Three tones, high, low and rising (BA), with lexical and inflectional minimal pairs; suffixed incorporated nouns lose inherent tone and accent, juxtaposed ones keep both. No fuller tone analysis.

tone.translation: The Otomi spoken in San Jerónimo Acazulco is a tonal language (high A, low B and rising BA), in which tone has both lexical functions (tö́htá 'uncle' vs. tö̀htá 'husband, old man') and inflectional ones (ngi nǜ 'you would see' vs. ngi nǘ 'he would see'). It is a head-marking language whose verbs take cross-reference markers for Subject and Object.
